title: Two formats, one data model
summary: JSON and YAML both describe trees of maps, lists, and scalars. Learn that model first and the syntax becomes notation for it.
text: You will meet these two formats everywhere a program needs settings or a message. `package.json`, `tsconfig.json`, and every REST API you call speak JSON. GitHub Actions workflows, Kubernetes manifests, Docker Compose files, and OpenAPI documents are usually YAML. They look different. Underneath, they describe the same kind of thing: a tree. ## The tree underneath Every JSON document is one value, and a value is one of six things: | Kind | JSON example | Notes | | --- | --- | --- | | object | `{"name": "api", "port": 8080}` | Unordered set of name/value pairs. YAML calls it a *mapping*. | | array | `[1, 2, 3]` | Ordered list. YAML calls it a *sequence*. | | string | `"hello"` | Always double-quoted in JSON. | | number | `8080`, `-1.5e3` | One number type. No separate integer or float. | | boolean | `true`, `false` | Lowercase only. | | null | `null` | The absence of a value. | Objects and arrays are containers. They hold other values, including other containers, so a document can nest as deep as you like. The other four are *scalars*: leaves of the tree. YAML has the same three building blocks: mappings, sequences, and scalars. It adds features JSON lacks (comments, anchors, several documents in one file, explicit type tags), but when a YAML file is loaded into a program, the result is almost always the same tree of maps, lists, strings, numbers, booleans, and nulls. That is the main idea of this course. **Learn the tree first. Treat the syntax as notation for it.** Most YAML bugs come from a gap between the tree the author pictured and the tree the parser built. ## One tree, three spellings Here is a small service description, written three ways. The script saves each spelling to a file and converts it to JSON with the course helper `yaml2json`. The `cmp` lines at the end compare the converted output byte for byte. Three things to notice: 1. `service.json` went through a **YAML** parser and came out unchanged. YAML 1.2 was designed so that JSON documents are valid YAML. 2. The *flow style* (`{...}` and `[...]`) is YAML's JSON-like notation. Inside flow style, YAML still lets you leave strings unquoted. 3. The *block style* uses indentation and `- ` for list items. This is what most YAML files you meet look like. ## Going the other way `json2yaml` reads strict JSON and writes block-style YAML. Lesson 17 covers what can and cannot survive a round trip. For plain data like this, nothing is lost. A sequence of mappings, written `- sku: A-1` followed by ` qty: 2`, often trips people up. The dash starts a list item, and that item is a mapping with two keys. Indentation is how you can tell `qty` belongs to the same item as `sku`. ## The tools used in this course Every example on this site was run by the build, and the stdout and stderr shown are what came back. The examples rely on a few commands: - `jq`, the command-line JSON processor, used from lesson 6 on. - `python3` and `node`, used where a language's own JSON library behaves in a way worth seeing. - Four small helpers in this repository's `tools/bin/`, each a thin wrapper around a published library: - `yaml2json` and `yamlcheck` use the [`yaml`](https://eemeli.org/yaml/) npm package, a YAML 1.2 parser that can also be switched to YAML 1.1 with `--yaml-1.1`. - `json2yaml` uses `JSON.parse` and then the same package's `stringify`. - `schema-check` uses [Ajv](https://ajv.js.org/) to validate against JSON Schema draft 2020-12. To run the examples yourself, clone the repository, run `npm ci`, and put the helpers on your `PATH`: The [playground](/playground) runs the same `yaml` package in your browser if you just want to try a snippet. The messages give `file:line:column` and an error code from the `yaml` package. They are also a first look at how a YAML parser reads indentation. `port` is indented under `name: api`, so the parser tries to treat `api` and the next line as one value, then finds a second `key:` inside it. title: The whole JSON grammar
summary: JSON is small enough to hold in your head. Learn what it allows, what it forbids, and why three parsers can disagree about the forbidden parts.
text: The JSON grammar fits on one page of RFC 8259. That is a feature. Every language has a parser for it, and the format has almost no room for dialects. In practice dialects appear anyway, mostly at the edges of the grammar. This lesson maps those edges. ## What the grammar allows A JSON text is **one value**, with optional whitespace around it. A value is an object, an array, a string, a number, `true`, `false`, or `null`. Older documentation says a top-level value must be an object or array. That was RFC 4627. RFC 8259 dropped the restriction, so `42` and `"hi"` are complete, valid JSON documents. Whitespace is four characters: space, tab, line feed, carriage return. It may appear between any two tokens and nowhere inside one. Objects and arrays separate their members with commas, and objects join name to value with a colon. That is all of it. The next script feeds the same top-level scalars to three parsers. `jq -c .` prints compact JSON, `node` uses `JSON.parse`, and Python uses `json.load`. All three agree. Note that `null` is a document too. A file whose entire content is `null` is valid, and a program that reads it must not assume it got an object. ## What the grammar forbids People bring habits from JavaScript, Python, and YAML. Each of these is **not** JSON: | Habit | Example | Why people try it | | --- | --- | --- | | Trailing comma | `{"a": 1,}` | Cleaner diffs when you add a line | | Single quotes | `{'a': 1}` | Python and JavaScript allow them | | Unquoted keys | `{a: 1}` | JavaScript object literals | | Leading zeros | `{"a": 01}` | Zero-padded IDs | | `NaN`, `Infinity` | `{"a": NaN}` | Floating-point results | | Comments | `// note` or `/* note */` | Config files | Run each one through all three parsers and look at what comes back. Read the output line by line: - The first three inputs are rejected by all three parsers. The messages differ in wording, but each points at a line and column, which is what you want when hunting a stray comma in a large file. - `01` is rejected by node and Python, but the installed **jq 1.6 accepts it and prints `1`**. A leading zero is not allowed by the grammar, so jq is being lenient. - `NaN` and `Infinity` are rejected by node. **Python accepts both** and prints them back. jq 1.6 accepts them too, but silently changes them: `NaN` became `null` and `Infinity` became the largest finite double, `1.7976931348623157e+308`. That last result is the dangerous one. A value that JSON cannot represent went in, and a different, valid-looking value came out, with exit status 0 and no warning. ## Making Python strict Python's `json` module accepts `NaN`, `Infinity`, and `-Infinity` by default. The `parse_constant` hook is called for those three names, and you can raise from it. Without the hook the document loads; with it, loading fails with the message from `reject`. If you write a service that accepts JSON from outside, pass this hook. The same module can also write the invalid value: `json.dumps(float("nan"))` produces `NaN`, which strict parsers then refuse. Pass `allow_nan=False` to `dumps` so that you find out at the sending end. ## Comments JSON has no comments. Crockford removed them on purpose, to stop people hiding parsing directives in them. Files such as `tsconfig.json` accept comments because TypeScript reads them with its own lenient parser (lesson [Config files](/lessons/config-files)), not because JSON allows them. The next script shows what the parsers here do with one. If you need a comment in data that must stay strict, the usual workaround is a key such as `"_comment"`, which the consumer is told to ignore. YAML has real comments, which is one reason people prefer it for files that humans edit (lesson [YAML structure](/lessons/yaml-structure)). ## Empty input is not a document An empty file contains no value, so it is not valid JSON. Node and Python report an error. jq 1.6 prints nothing and exits 0, so a pipeline can carry on with an empty result and no failure. Check what y

title: Strings, escapes, and Unicode
summary: A JSON string is a quoted run of Unicode characters with a short list of escapes. The surprises are in how languages count its length and what they do with bytes that are not valid text.
text: A JSON string starts and ends with a double quote. Between the quotes can be any Unicode character except the double quote, the backslash, and the control characters U+0000 through U+001F. Those must be written as escapes. ## The escapes | Written | Meaning | | --- | --- | | `\"` | double quote | | `\\` | backslash | | `\/` | forward slash (allowed, never required) | | `\b` `\f` `\n` `\r` `\t` | backspace, form feed, line feed, carriage return, tab | | `\uXXXX` | the UTF-16 code unit with that four-digit hex value | No other backslash sequence is legal. In particular there is no `\x41`, no `\'`, and no way to break a string over two lines. The script below stores one string that uses most of them, then reads it three ways. `jq -r` prints the raw string without JSON quoting. `jq -c` prints it as JSON again. `jq -a` prints JSON with every non-ASCII character escaped. Compare the file with the `jq -c` line. The escape `\u00e9` turned into the real character `é`, and the pair `\ud83d\ude00` became a single emoji. The optional `\/` became a plain `/`. Writing the escapes and writing the characters are two spellings of the same string. ## Surrogate pairs `\uXXXX` names a UTF-16 code unit, which is 16 bits. Characters above U+FFFF, such as most emoji, do not fit, so JSON writes them as two escapes: a high surrogate (`\ud83d`) followed by a low surrogate (`\ude00`). Together they mean U+1F600. A decoder must combine them. A lone surrogate is not a character at all. That history explains a famous inconsistency. Each example runs in its own empty directory, so this script recreates the same file first. It then measures the string in Python and in node. Python counts code points, so the emoji is one. JavaScript's `.length` counts UTF-16 units, so the emoji is two. Spreading the string into an array walks code points, which brings node back to Python's answer. A length limit written in one language and checked in the other is a bug waiting for its first emoji. ## ensure_ascii When Python writes JSON, `json.dumps` escapes every non-ASCII character by default (`ensure_ascii=True`). That keeps the output pure ASCII, which is safe over any channel, but it makes the text hard to read and larger. Pass `ensure_ascii=False` to write real UTF-8. Both lines decode to the same string. jq goes the other way: it writes UTF-8 by default and escapes only when you pass `-a`, as the first example showed. ## Control characters must be escaped A literal tab or newline inside a string is not allowed. The next script writes a document with a real tab character in the string and asks each parser what it thinks. All three refuse by default. Python's `strict=False` switch lets control characters through. It exists for convenience with sloppy producers, and using it means your parser accepts text that other parsers will reject. ## Encoding: UTF-8, no byte order mark RFC 8259 says JSON exchanged between systems must be UTF-8. It also says implementations must not add a byte order mark (BOM, the bytes `EF BB BF`) and may choose to ignore one. Two real-world problems follow: files saved by some Windows editors start with a BOM, and files that are not UTF-8 at all sneak in. The results split. The installed jq 1.6 accepts the BOM. Python and node both refuse it, and Python's message tells you to open the file as `utf-8-sig`. For the invalid byte, Python raises a decode error, while jq 1.6 prints a replacement character (`�`, U+FFFD) and carries on. Silent replacement loses data, so a pipeline that must not alter its input should decode strictly. A lone surrogate is another gap in the specification: `"\ud83d"` is grammatically fine, but it is not a valid Unicode string. Python and JavaScript both load it, while jq 1.6 rejects it with a parse error about a bad surrogate pair escape. Do not rely on any behaviour for that input. ## Exercises

title: Numbers, precision, and big IDs
summary: JSON has one number type and says nothing about its size or precision. What you get back depends on the language that reads it, and large integers are where tools quietly disagree.
text: The number grammar is short: an optional minus sign, an integer part with no leading zeros, an optional fraction, and an optional exponent. `0`, `-12`, `3.14`, and `6.02e23` are numbers. `01`, `.5`, `5.`, `+1`, and `0x1F` are not (lesson [The whole JSON grammar](/lessons/json-grammar)). There is **one** number type. JSON does not distinguish an integer from a float, or a 32-bit value from a 64-bit one. It also does not say how many digits you may use. The text `9007199254740993` is a legal number. What a program does with it is the reader's decision. ## Three readers, one document The next script reads one document in jq, node, and Python and prints what each holds. The `id` is 2^53 + 1, the first positive integer that a 64-bit double cannot store exactly. Read the three lines against the input: - **node and jq 1.6** hold every number as a 64-bit double. `id` came back as `9007199254740992`, one lower than what was written, with no warning. `big` was rounded to the nearest double. `pi` lost its trailing digits in all three tools, because the digits after the 17th are beyond any double. - **Python** reads a number without a fraction or exponent as an arbitrary-precision `int`, so `id` and `big` came back exactly. - `1.0` and `1E2` have a fraction or exponent, so Python reads them as floats and writes `1.0` and `100.0`. node and jq print `1` and `100`, because for them the two spellings were always the same number. Notice what this means for round trips. Python preserved the text of `id` and `big` because it treats integers specially, not because JSON promises it. ## Doing arithmetic with doubles Double precision is a property of the arithmetic too, not only the parser. `0.1 + 0.2` is `0.30000000000000004` everywhere, because none of these languages can store 0.1 exactly in binary. `2**53 + 1` is where they split. node's `Number` rounds it, and the constant `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` tells you the largest integer below which every integer is exact. Python's `int` has no such limit, but converting that value to `float` rounds it, as the last line of its output shows. jq 1.6 does the sum with doubles. ## Identifiers: use strings Twitter's API famously returns each tweet ID twice, as `id` (a number) and `id_str` (a string), because JavaScript clients corrupted the numeric form. The lesson generalises: if a value is an identifier rather than a quantity, you never add or compare it by size, so a string loses nothing and cannot be rounded. The string survives untouched. The number does not: its digits are different after parsing, and the comparison in node prints `false`. Converting a string to a number reintroduces the rounding, because `tonumber` in jq 1.6 produces a double. ## Keeping exact decimals in Python Python's `json` module lets you choose how numbers are built. `parse_float=Decimal` keeps the digits you typed, including trailing zeros, which matters for prices and measurements. `1.10` stays `Decimal('1.10')`. Writing a `Decimal` back out takes an extra step, because `json.dumps` does not know the type. Pass a `default=` function or convert to a string. Many teams solve the problem on the wire instead and send money as an integer count of cents, or as a string such as `"1.10"`. ## Out-of-range numbers A document may contain `1e400`, which is a legal number that no double can hold. Readers handle it in different ways. The next script shows the three here. jq 1.6 clamps to the largest finite double. node reads it as `Infinity`, and `JSON.stringify` then writes `null`, because JSON has no way to write infinity. Python reads `inf` and `json.dumps` writes `Infinity`, which is not valid JSON (lesson [The whole JSON grammar](/lessons/json-grammar)). In each case a legal input turned into something else without an error. ## Exercises

title: Objects, duplicate keys, and ordering
summary: A JSON object looks like a dictionary, but the grammar is looser than any dictionary type. Duplicate keys, key order, and the difference between null and missing all behave differently from what you might assume.
text: An object is a set of name/value pairs. The grammar requires the names to be strings. It does not require them to be unique, and it says nothing about order. The RFC's wording is that names **should** be unique. Software is free to do something else, and it does. ## Duplicate keys The script below parses `{"a":1,"b":2,"a":3}` with four tools: jq, node, Python, and the course's `yaml2json` helper, which is a YAML parser reading the JSON. jq, node, and Python all return `{"a":3,"b":2}`: the **last** value wins, and the key keeps the position of its first appearance. That agreement is a convention, and not one you can rely on in every library. The YAML parser takes the opposite view. It reports `DUPLICATE_KEY` with a position and the helper exits with status 1. YAML 1.2 requires keys to be unique, so a parser that rejects the duplicate is following its specification. Python can also be made strict. `json.load` calls an `object_pairs_hook` with the list of pairs before it builds the dictionary, and that list still contains both entries. The example is deliberately a security-shaped one. If one component reads `role` as `user` and another as `admin`, you have a vulnerability, and the usual cause is two parsers with different rules about the same bytes. ## Key order An object is unordered, so no program should depend on key order. That does not mean order is invisible. Parsers preserve it differently, and diffs, hashes, and signatures all see the bytes. jq and Python write keys back in the order they were read. `jq -S` and `sort_keys=True` sort them, at every level, which is how you make two documents comparable with `diff`. node is the surprise: it put `"0"` and `"1"` **first**, in numeric order, ahead of the other keys. JavaScript objects order integer-like keys before string keys, and `JSON.parse` builds ordinary objects. Any order you saw in a JavaScript client for numeric keys is the language's, not the document's. For stable output, sort keys before you hash, sign, or diff. Lesson [Converting between YAML and JSON](/lessons/converting) uses `jq -S` for exactly this. ## null is not missing `{"a": null}` and `{}` are different documents. A key set to `null` exists. A missing key does not. Whether your language shows the difference depends on how you ask. Reading `.a` and `.b` in jq gives `null` for both, but `has` tells them apart. Python's `d.get` returns `None` for both, while `in` shows which exists. In node, reading the missing key gives `undefined`, a value JSON cannot write, so `JSON.stringify` drops the key `x` altogether and keeps `y`. Notice also that jq's `//` operator replaces both `null` and `false` with its default, so `.a // "dflt"` treats a present-but-null key like a missing one. Choose a convention for your own formats and document it. Some APIs treat `null` as "clear this field" and a missing key as "leave it alone", and that distinction is what makes partial updates work. ## Empty containers `{}` and `[]` are valid values and are not `null`. They are what you get from an object with no members or a list with no items. Both have length 0, the two are not equal to each other, and neither equals `null`. The last line shows `del` removing a key: deleting `a` from `{"a":null}` leaves `{}`, a different document from `{"a":null}`. ## Exercises

title: jq basics
summary: jq is a small language for taking JSON apart. Learn paths, the iterator, pipes, select, and the options that make it usable in shell scripts.
text: `jq` reads JSON, runs a **filter** over it, and prints the result. Every filter takes one input and produces zero or more outputs. Everything in jq, from selecting a field to building a report, is a filter combined with other filters. The installed jq here is **1.6**. The examples were run on it, and the manual at jqlang.org covers newer versions too, so check `jq --version` when a feature from the manual is missing. All the examples in this lesson use the same input, a small team description. Each script recreates it first. ## Paths and the iterator A dot is the identity filter, and it prints its input, pretty-printed. `.team` reads a field. `.members[0]` reads an array element, and `.members[]` produces **every** element, one output each. `-r` is **raw output**. Without it strings print with their JSON quotes (`"core"`), and with it they print as plain text (`core`), which is what you want to pass to another command. `-c` is **compact output**: one line per result instead of the indented layout. `.members[1:]` is a slice, like Python's, and a negative index counts from the end. ## Pipes and select The pipe `|` sends each output of the left filter into the right filter. `.members[] | .name` is the same as `.members[].name`. The filter `select(condition)` passes its input through when the condition is true and produces nothing when it is false, so it works as a filter on a stream. `{name}` is shorthand for `{name: .name}`. `keys` returns an object's keys in **sorted** order, not file order. `length` of an array is its element count. ## Missing fields and errors Asking an object for a key it lacks gives `null`, not an error. Asking the wrong *kind* of value for a key or index, such as indexing a number, is an error. The `//` operator supplies a default, and `?` suppresses an error. The first command shows `null` for the entry with no email. The default operator replaced it with `"none"`. Indexing the number `1` with `[0]` is an error: jq prints `jq: error ... Cannot index number with number` and exits with status 5. Adding `?` swallows the error. The filter produces no output at all and the exit status is 0, which is convenient, but it also hides real mistakes, so use it deliberately. ## Exit status for scripts By default jq's exit status says whether it could run, not what it found. With `-e` (`--exit-status`), jq exits with 1 when the last output was `false` or `null`, and with 4 when there was no output at all. That lets an `if` in a shell script test the data. `@tsv` and `@csv` format an array as a tab- or comma-separated row. They are the safe way to print columns, because they quote and escape the values, unlike `echo "$a,$b"`. ## Passing values in `--arg name value` binds `$name` to a **string**. `--argjson name json` binds it to a parsed JSON value, so numbers stay numbers. Neither needs any quoting inside the filter. The `-n` flag runs the filter with no input, which is useful when you only want to build a value. `--arg n 3` creates the string `"3"`, so the last line converts it before doing arithmetic. ## Exercises

title: Reshaping JSON with jq
summary: Build new objects, summarise arrays, rewrite values, and edit a file safely. These are the jq patterns that replace most throwaway scripts.
text: Lesson [jq basics](/lessons/jq-basics) used jq to read values out. This lesson uses it to produce new JSON. The same input is used throughout: four orders, each with a customer, a total, and a list of items. Every script recreates it. ## Building new values An object construction `{a: .x, b: .y}` makes a new object from parts of the input. An array construction `[...]` collects every output of a filter into a list. `map(f)` is shorthand for `[.[] | f]`. `{id}` is shorthand for `{id: .id}`. The expression `"\(...)"` is string interpolation, handy with `-r` for readable lines. ## Grouping and summing `group_by(.key)` sorts an array and splits it into runs that share a key. Each group is an array, so you can summarise it with another `map`. `sort_by` accepts several keys, and a negative sign reverses a number. `reduce SOURCE as $x (START; UPDATE)` folds a stream into one value. Here the start is `{}`, and `.[$o.cust] += $o.total` adds each order's total into the entry for its customer, creating it when it is missing. Look at the last result. Using `add` on one-key objects *merges* them, so the later `ada` entry replaced the earlier one: `55.5` instead of `85.5`. `add` sums numbers and concatenates arrays, but on objects it merges. When you need a sum per key, use `group_by` or `reduce`. ## Objects as lists of entries `to_entries` turns an object into `[{"key": ..., "value": ...}, ...]`, which you can filter and sort like any array. `from_entries` turns it back. `with_entries(f)` does the round trip for you, and `map_values(f)` changes every value. Reach for `to_entries` whenever you need to filter an object by its keys or values. Most jq reports over a dictionary, such as "keys that start with `x_`", are one `to_entries | map(select(...)) | from_entries` away. ## Updates and deletes `.path = value` sets a path. `.path |= f` applies a filter to the current value at that path. `del(.path)` removes one. Updates operate on a copy and print the result, since jq never modifies its input file. ## Slurping By default jq runs the filter once per top-level value in its input. With `-s` (`--slurp`) it first collects every value into one array and runs the filter once. That turns a file of separate documents into something you can sum or sort (lesson [JSON Lines](/lessons/json-lines) builds on this). ## Editing a file safely Because the shell opens the output file before jq starts, redirecting onto the input is a mistake. The next script shows the failure, then the correct pattern. The wrong version left a zero-byte file and no error. The safe version writes the new content beside the original and replaces it in one `mv`, which is atomic when both names are in the same directory. If jq fails, the `&&` stops before `mv`, and the original stays intact. ## Exercises

title: JSON Lines for logs and streams
summary: One JSON value per line turns a log or an export into something you can stream, grep, and append to. Learn the format, the jq and Python patterns for it, and what each tool does when one line is bad.
text: A normal JSON file holds one value, so a parser has to read the whole file before it can give you anything. A log with a million events as a single JSON array is awkward: you cannot append to it without rewriting the closing bracket, and you cannot read the first record until the last byte arrives. **JSON Lines** (also called NDJSON, newline-delimited JSON) fixes that with one rule: each line is a complete JSON value, usually an object, and lines are separated by `\n`. Because a compact JSON value never contains a raw newline (lesson [Strings, escapes, and Unicode](/lessons/json-strings)), splitting on newlines is always safe. Appending a record is appending a line. `head`, `tail`, `grep`, and `wc -l` all work on it. ## Reading a stream with jq jq already treats its input as a stream of values. A filter runs once for each one, and `-c` prints each result on its own line, so the output is JSON Lines again. With `-s` (slurp), jq reads every record into one array first. That gives you `length`, `group_by`, and `add`, at the price of holding the whole file in memory. Without it, jq handles one record at a time, so memory stays flat on a very large file. Pretty-printed objects are still valid input to jq, because it does not care about line boundaries. The format is a convention for *writers* and for line-based tools. A file written with an indented `jq .` is not JSON Lines, even though jq can read it. ## A bad line in the middle Real logs contain truncated writes, stack traces, and stray text. Here is a file whose third line is not JSON. Read the output carefully. jq printed the first two records, reported a parse error that names line 3, exited with status 4, and **never printed the fourth record**. The parser cannot resynchronise after a syntax error in a stream, so everything after the bad line is lost. With `-s` it is worse: no records at all are printed, because the array is never completed. If you cannot guarantee clean input, read the file as plain text with `-R` (`--raw-input`) and decode each line yourself with `fromjson`. Wrapping it in `try` lets you decide what happens to a failure. The first command drops line 3 and carries on, so all three valid records produce output. The second keeps a marker for the bad line in the output stream, which is easier to audit. Both read all four lines, unlike the plain version. ## The same job in Python and node In a general-purpose language you control the loop, so you can number the lines and decide for each failure. Python's file object yields one line at a time, which keeps memory low. Python reports the failure on line 3 and goes on to line 4. The same loop works in node when you split the text on newlines and call `JSON.parse` in a `try`. The next script also shows what happens if you hand the whole `.jsonl` file to a JSON parser as if it were one document. Both parsers read the first record and then fail on what follows it, with a message about extra data. This is the usual first symptom when a service is pointed at a `.jsonl` file and expects a JSON document. ## Writing JSON Lines Writers must emit compact JSON and end every record with a newline, including the last. A file whose final line lacks the newline works in most readers, but `wc -l` will then count one fewer record than there are. Use `jq -c` or `json.dumps` with its default separators, and never pretty-print. ## Exercises

title: Block structure and indentation
summary: Mappings, sequences, and nesting in block style. The indentation rules are short, and nearly every beginner error is one of three mistakes.
text: In lesson 1 you saw that YAML and JSON describe the same tree. This lesson is about the block notation that makes YAML look like YAML: no braces, no brackets, structure carried by line breaks and indentation. ## The three building blocks A **block mapping** is a set of `key: value` lines that start in the same column. A **block sequence** is a set of `- item` lines that start in the same column. A value can be a scalar, or another mapping or sequence on the following lines, indented further. The `owner` key has no value on its own line, so its value is whatever block comes next, one level deeper. The `ports` key does the same with a sequence. There is no separate end marker: a block ends when a line appears at a shallower column. ## The indentation rules The rules are short: 1. **Spaces only.** A tab cannot be used for indentation. 2. **Siblings share a column.** All keys of one mapping start at the same column. All items of one sequence do too. 3. **A child is indented more than its parent.** How much more is up to you, as long as you stay consistent within that block. Two spaces is the convention. 4. **`- ` counts as indentation.** The dash and the space after it take up two columns, and whatever follows the dash starts at the third. The fourth rule explains the most common surprise. A sequence that is the value of a key is allowed to start at the *same column as the key*: Both spellings are valid. Style guides disagree about which to use, so follow whatever the file you are editing already does. Kubernetes manifests often leave sequences unindented; GitHub workflows usually indent them. ## Lists of mappings When a list item is a mapping, the first key can sit on the same line as the dash. The remaining keys line up under it, which is the column after `- `: The first item uses the compact form and the second puts the dash alone. They produce the same kind of tree. The compact form is much more common because the dash points at the start of each record. A sequence directly inside a sequence also works, using two dashes on one line, as the last command shows. ## Flow collections inside block style You can mix the two. A value in a block mapping may be written in flow style (`[...]` or `{...}`), which is handy for short lists: Note `no_value:`. A key with nothing after it becomes `null`, not an empty string and not an empty mapping. Lesson 11 returns to this. ## The three common mistakes The first file uses a tab, the second has a key at column 2 beside a sibling at column 3, and the third has a list item indented deeper than its neighbour. Each message gives a line and column and a short code from the `yaml` package. `TAB_AS_INDENT` and `BAD_INDENT` say what is wrong. The third message is less direct. The parser sees `- 1` start a sequence at column 4, then sees `- 2` at column 3, which cannot belong to that sequence and cannot be a key either. Its error names a block sequence used as an implicit map key. When a YAML error reads strangely, look at the indentation of the line it points at and the line above it. The quiet version of the same mistake is worse. Here the second item is indented *one space further* than the first: The file is valid, and `a` has one item, the string `"1 - 2"`. The extra-indented line was read as a continuation of the first item's text, folded onto one line with a space. Lesson 10 explains this folding rule. For now: if your list has the wrong number of items, convert it and look. ## Exercises

title: Strings, quoting, and multi-line text
summary: YAML has five ways to write a string. Know when plain text is safe, what forces quotes, and how the block styles | and > treat line breaks.
text: JSON has one way to write a string. YAML has five: plain, single-quoted, double-quoted, literal block, and folded block. They all produce the same kind of value, a string, but they differ in what they let you type. This lesson gets you from "I quote everything to be safe" to knowing when each style is the right tool. ## Plain, single-quoted, double-quoted Read the output against the input: - **Plain** has no quotes at all. The text is taken as written, with surrounding spaces trimmed. - **Single-quoted** has exactly one escape: two single quotes in a row mean one quote. A backslash is just a backslash, which is why `'no\tescape here'` came out with a literal `\t`. JSON shows that as `\\t`. - **Double-quoted** supports backslash escapes such as `\t`, `\xNN`, and `\uNNNN`, much like JSON strings. Use it when you need a tab, a newline, or a non-printing character. Single quotes are the better default when the text contains backslashes, such as a regular expression or a Windows path. Nothing needs escaping except the quote itself. A workable habit: write plain scalars for ordinary words and identifiers, single quotes when the text has backslashes or looks like something else, and double quotes only when you need an escape. Quoting is also how you tell the parser "this is a string" when plain text would be read as another type. That second use matters more than it seems, and lesson 11 is built around it. ## What forces quotes A plain scalar is not just "anything". The parser treats some characters specially at the start of a value, and some sequences anywhere: The first block shows quoting working. `a#b` is fine because the comment marker `#` only counts when a space comes before it, so `comment_after: a #b` is the string `a` followed by a comment. The second part runs each risky value unquoted and prints the first message. Each one fails: `@` and `%` are reserved indicator characters, `x: y` looks like a nested mapping, `- x` looks like a list item on the key's line, `[x` opens a flow sequence that never closes, and a bare `*` is an alias with no name. The practical rule: quote any value that starts with one of ``@ ` * & ! | > % { [ ' "`` , contains `: ` or ` #`, or that you would not want read as a number, boolean, or null. The last case is the subject of lesson 11. ## Literal blocks: keep the line breaks A `|` after the key starts a **literal** block. The indented lines that follow become the value, line breaks and all. This is what you want for shell scripts, certificates, and anything where lines matter. ## Folded blocks: join lines into paragraphs A `>` starts a **folded** block. A single line break becomes a space, a blank line becomes a real newline, and lines that are indented *more* than the rest keep their break. It suits long prose you want to wrap in the source file. In the literal value the second line keeps its two extra spaces. In the folded value, `folded text` and `continues here` merged into one line, and the blank line became `\n`. ## Chomping: controlling the trailing newlines By default (called *clip*) a block scalar ends with exactly one newline, no matter how many blank lines follow it. Two indicators on the header change that: - `|-` or `>-` (*strip*) removes the final newline. - `|+` or `>+` (*keep*) keeps every trailing blank line. An *indentation indicator* is a digit, as in `|2`. It sets the indentation explicitly, which you need when the first line of the content starts with spaces that would otherwise be taken as indentation. `keep` ended in three newlines: the one that ends the line, plus the two blank lines. `indicator` begins with two spaces because the indicator `2` said the indentation is two columns and the line has four. ## Multi-line plain scalars A plain scalar can also wrap across lines, using the same folding rule as `>`: The first break became a space and the blank line became a newline. This is how the quiet bug in lesson 9 happened: an over-indented `- 2` was read as more text for the p

title: Implicit types and the Norway problem
summary: An unquoted YAML value is a string only if it fails to look like something else. See what YAML 1.2 and YAML 1.1 each turn into numbers, booleans, and nulls, and how quoting stops it.
text:
JSON values carry their type in their spelling: quotes mean string, digits mean number, `true` means boolean. A YAML scalar does not need quotes, so the parser has to *guess* the type of an unquoted value from its text. The rules for guessing are the YAML **schema**, and there are two you will meet. ## Two sets of rules - **YAML 1.2 Core schema** is what the `yaml2json` helper uses by default. It recognises `null`, `~`, an empty value, `true`/`false` in a few capitalisations, decimal integers, floats, and `0x` hex and `0o` octal. - **YAML 1.1** has a larger set. It also treats `yes`, `no`, `on`, `off`, `y`, `n` as booleans, reads a leading `0` as octal, and reads `1:30` as a number in base 60. Some very widely used libraries still implement 1.1. PyYAML is the best-known example. The helper takes `--yaml-1.1` to switch. Here is one file read both ways: Compare the two lines: - **`countries`.** Under 1.1 the second item, `NO`, became `false`. This is the **Norway problem**: a list of ISO country codes loses Norway because `NO` looks like "no". - **`switches`.** Under 1.2 only `true` and `false` are booleans, so the six words stay strings. Under 1.1 all six become booleans. - **`octal_looking`.** `010` is 10 under 1.2 (a decimal with a leading zero) and 8 under 1.1. An octal literal in 1.2 must be written `0o10`, and in 1.1 that is not a number, so it stays the string `"0o10"`. - **`duration`.** `1:30` is the string `"1:30"` under 1.2 and the number 90 under 1.1 (one minute thirty seconds, counted in base 60). - **`version`.** Both give `3.1`. `3.10` is a float in either schema, and the trailing zero is not kept. A version that must read `3.10` has to be a string. The version case is not a YAML 1.1 quirk. It follows from the number rule alone, which makes it a common source of bugs in CI matrices, where `python: [3.8, 3.9, 3.10]` loses the last one's identity. A note on the word "guess". The resolution of types happens in the parser, before your program sees the data. By the time you hold a value in memory, nothing records whether the author wrote `no` or `false`, or `010` or `10`. A bug that comes from the wrong guess cannot be fixed afterwards in application code, because the information is already gone. It has to be fixed in the source file or in the parser settings. ## The key `on` The same schema difference changes keys, not just values: Under 1.1 the key `on` became the string `"true"`, because JSON keys must be strings and the boolean `true` has to be spelled somehow. GitHub Actions workflows start with `on:`, so this is a known trap when you load a workflow with a 1.1 library. Lesson 18 returns to it. ## Nulls, empties, and special floats Three spellings of null agree: `~`, nothing at all, and the word `null`. A missing value is `null`, not an empty string. If you want an empty string, write `''`. Two lines of the output deserve care: - **`inf` and `nan`.** Both schemas parse `.inf` and `.nan` into real floating-point infinity and not-a-number, but **JSON cannot represent either**. The helper's `JSON.stringify` step wrote `null` for both, so the output does not distinguish them from a true null. Treat that as a limit of converting to JSON, not as the YAML meaning. - **`date`.** YAML 1.2 Core leaves `2024-01-15` as a string. YAML 1.1 has a timestamp type, so the library turned it into a date object, which appears in JSON as `"2024-01-15T00:00:00.000Z"`, with a time and a time zone that were never in the source. ## The fix: say what you mean Quoting always gives a string, in any version. An explicit tag does the same: Both parsers give the same result now. That is the property you want from config that other people's tools will read. Many teams adopt a simple convention: quote every string that could be mistaken for another type, and run a schema check ([JSON Schema basics](/lessons/json-schema-basics)) so a value of the wrong type is caught on load, not in production. ## Exercises yaml
flags: [on, off]
region: no
build

title: Anchors, aliases, and merge keys
summary: Anchors let one YAML node be reused in several places. Learn what an alias means, what disappears when you convert to JSON, and why the merge key behaves differently depending on the YAML version.
text: JSON has no way to say "this value is the same as that one". If two services share a configuration, you write it twice. YAML adds a feature for this: mark a node with an **anchor** and refer to it later with an **alias**. This lesson covers what that does, what it does not do, and the related merge key that many files rely on. ## Anchor and alias An anchor is `&name` placed before a node. An alias is `*name`, and it stands for the anchored node. An alias can refer to a scalar or to a whole collection. The rule is that the anchor must appear earlier in the file than the alias that uses it. A name with no anchor is an error. Check it with `yaml2json` here, because it is the conversion step that resolves aliases and reports the failure: ## Aliases become copies in JSON In a YAML parser's memory, an alias can point at the *same* object as its anchor. JSON has no such notion, so on conversion every alias becomes a full, independent copy. The output above shows `"other": ["a","b"]` written out twice, once under `list` and once under `other`. The sharing is gone. Two consequences follow: - Converting YAML to JSON and back does **not** restore the anchors. The result is longer and has no reuse. See [Converting between formats](/lessons/converting). - Anchors are a feature of the *file*. If your program loads the YAML and edits one copy, whether the other changes depends on how the library represents aliases. Do not count on either behaviour. You can reuse a name. A later anchor with the same name replaces the earlier one for aliases that come after it: `b` got 1 and `d` got 2. It parses, but it is a confusing thing to write. ## The merge key Copying a whole mapping is useful, but the common need is "all of these defaults, with two changes". The merge key `<<` does that: its value is a mapping (or a list of mappings) whose keys are added to the current one. The merge key is where YAML versions diverge, so the same file is read both ways: Under YAML 1.1, `svc` got `retries` from `base`, and its own `timeout: 60` took priority over the merged 30. Under 1.2 (the helper's default) nothing was merged: `svc` has a key literally named `<<`, whose value is a copy of `base`. No error is reported, which is why the pitfall above matters. So what do real tools do? Support varies between libraries and between settings of one library. When you write a file that uses `<<`, find out what the program that loads it does, and test it, as this lesson does. ## Which value wins With a list of mappings, earlier entries take priority. An explicit key in the mapping itself beats every merged one. `first_wins` has `k: 1` because `p` came first in the list, and `reversed` has `k: 2` for the same reason. Both have all three of `k`, `other`, and `extra`, since the merge adds keys that are missing. `explicit` has `k: 9`: the key written in the mapping itself overrides the merged one. The merge is **shallow**. If the merged mapping contains a nested mapping or list and you set the same top-level key, the whole value is replaced, not combined: `over.env` is `{"B": 2}`. The `A: 1` from the defaults is gone, and `tags` was kept. If you need a deep merge, do it explicitly in code, or with `jq`'s `*` operator ([jq transforms](/lessons/jq-transform)). ## When to use them Anchors earn their place when the same block repeats three or more times and must stay identical, such as the shared steps in a CI file or the common settings of several services. They cost readability: a reader has to scroll up to find what `*base` means, and an edit to the anchor changes every use. Two or three repeated lines are usually clearer written out. If a tool validates the file against a schema ([JSON Schema basics](/lessons/json-schema-basics)), validate the *resolved* data, because that is what the program will see. ## Exercises

title: Documents, comments, directives, and tags
summary: A YAML file is a stream that can hold several documents. Learn the document markers, where comments are allowed, what a %YAML directive does, and how a parser treats tags it does not know.
text:
A JSON file is one value. A YAML file is a **stream** of zero or more documents, and each document is one value. Most files have a single document, but multi-document files are routine: Kubernetes manifests and many log formats use them. ## Document markers A line of three dashes, `---`, starts a document. A line of three dots, `...`, ends one. The start marker is optional for the first document and required to separate the rest. The end marker is rarely needed, since the next `---` also ends the previous document. By default `yaml2json` refuses a stream with more than one document, because a single JSON value cannot hold three. `--all` collects them into a JSON array in order. `yamlcheck` counts them: three documents, with the `...` end marker making no difference to the count. A JSON consumer cannot read a stream, so multi-document YAML is usually split first, or converted with `--all` and processed as an array. Lesson 19 does this with a Kubernetes-style file. ## Comments A `#` starts a comment **only when it follows whitespace or begins a line**. Inside quotes, or glued to other text, it is just a character: `a` is `1` with the comment stripped, `b` is the string `"2#not a comment"`, and `c` keeps the `#` inside the quotes. JSON has no comments at all, so converting to JSON discards them. They are not in the tree. One practical habit follows from the stream rule. When you receive a YAML file from someone else, count its documents before assuming it is one value. `yamlcheck` prints the count, and a file that you expected to hold a single configuration but that reports two is usually a sign of a stray `---` in the middle of a copy-and-paste. ## Directives A line beginning with `%` before the `---` is a **directive**. The one you will see is `%YAML`, which declares the YAML version of the document. A parser that supports several versions uses it to choose rules. Here the helper runs in its default 1.2 mode, yet the directive changes the outcome: Under `%YAML 1.1`, `no` became `false`, even though no `--yaml-1.1` flag was passed. This is the Norway problem from [lesson 11](/lessons/yaml-types), switched on by the file itself. A version the parser does not know, like 1.3, produced a `BAD_DIRECTIVE` warning from `yamlcheck`, and the document was still read. Directives are rare in practice. Most files carry none, which means the version comes from the library that loads them. ## Tags A **tag** says what type a node is, written before the value with `!`. YAML defines a set of standard tags, spelled `!!` followed by a name. The ones that matter: `!!str`, `!!int`, `!!float`, `!!bool`, `!!null`, and `!!binary`. Beyond those, anyone can define their own, such as `!Ref` and `!Sub` in AWS CloudFormation templates. Read the output carefully: - `!!int "42"` forced the quoted text to the number 42, and `!!str 42` forced the number to the string `"42"`. `!!bool "true"` and `!!null ""` converted the text in the same way. So a tag can *change* the type that guessing would pick, which is why `!!str` is the heavy-duty alternative to quoting. - The three CloudFormation tags did not fail. `!Ref MyBucket` is the string `"MyBucket"`, `!GetAtt [Res, Arn]` is a list of two strings, and `!Sub` kept its text unchanged. **The tags are gone from the JSON.** - `yamlcheck` reports a `TAG_RESOLVE_FAILED` warning for each of the three, and still says the document is fine. `yaml2json` printed nothing to stderr and exited 0. A warning is easy to miss, and a converter has no obligation to show it. The consequence is the one in the pitfall above. A generic loader gives you the values but not the meaning, so a CloudFormation file converted this way no longer says which strings are references. ## Exercises yaml
x: 10 #ten
y: 10#ten
z: "10 #ten"

title: Loading untrusted YAML safely
summary: YAML's power is also its attack surface: tags that construct objects, alias expansion that exhausts memory, and silent surprises like duplicate keys. Learn the habit that covers them.
text: Everything so far assumed you wrote the file. A YAML file that arrives from a user, a pull request, or an upload is **untrusted input**, and YAML needs more care than JSON here because it is a richer language. This lesson covers the specific ways it goes wrong and the small number of habits that prevent them. ## Risk 1: tags that build objects A tag names a type, and some loaders let a tag name a *type in the host language*. This is a documented behaviour of PyYAML. Its full loader, `yaml.load` with an unsafe loader class, can construct arbitrary Python objects from tags such as `!!python/object/apply:...`, and that includes calling functions. For that reason PyYAML's documentation tells you to use `yaml.safe_load` for any input you do not control, which accepts only the standard YAML types. Treating `load` as an alias for `safe_load` is the classic mistake. Libraries in other languages that can build native objects from tags carry the same class of risk, so the advice is the same everywhere. This course does not run such a payload. What we can show safely is what a *generic, safe* parser does with the same text: The `yaml` package does not know a `python/object/apply` tag. It reported an unresolved tag, dropped it, and returned the argument list as plain data. Nothing was called, since this parser has no mechanism for constructing objects from tags. That is what "safe" means in practice: the document can only produce maps, lists, strings, numbers, booleans, and nulls. Rule one: use the safe entry point of whichever library you have, and never enable object construction for input you did not write. ## Risk 2: aliases that expand Lesson 12 showed that an alias is a copy in JSON. That means a small document can describe a very large one. Here each level lists the previous level nine times: The file is 237 bytes, as the first line of output shows. Fully expanded, `f` alone holds 531441 strings. This is the "billion laughs" attack, and a parser that expands it naively can use gigabytes of memory. The `yaml` package guards against this with a limit, `maxAliasCount`, and `yaml2json` exposes it as `--max-alias-count`. The default rejected the file above with a clear message. The same limit is useful in the other direction too: you can lower it for small, hand-written configs. The 64 strings in `small.yaml` pass the default limit and fail a limit of 10. Pick a limit that is generous for your legitimate files and far from what an attacker would want. Other libraries have different defaults, or none. Check yours. Size limits matter too, but they belong outside the parser: cap the upload size, and cap nesting depth if your loader exposes it. ## Risk 3: duplicate keys A mapping with the same key twice is ambiguous. JSON's RFC says names SHOULD be unique and does not say what a parser must do, so different tools disagree. YAML 1.2 requires keys to be unique, and the `yaml` package reports an error: `yamlcheck` flagged both files, but `jq` printed `{"role":"admin"}` without complaint: the last value won. This is a security issue, not a style point. If one component validates the first value and another uses the last, an attacker can show each component a different answer. Rejecting duplicate keys at parse time closes that gap. For more on this see [JSON objects](/lessons/json-objects). ## The habit: safe parse, then validate Safe loading tells you the data has the shape of plain maps and lists. It does not tell you the *contents* are right. Add a second step, which is to check the result against a schema, covered in [JSON Schema basics](/lessons/json-schema-basics): The good file passes. The bad one fails three checks at once: wrong role, a port that is a string, and an extra key. All three are things a safe parser accepts happily. The `|| echo` shows the exit status is non-zero, which is what a CI step or upload handler can act on. Each step catches a different thing. The safe loader stops code execution, the alias limit stops memory exha

title: JSON Schema, the basics
summary: A schema is a JSON document that says what other documents must look like. Write one, run it, and learn to read the errors.
text: A parser answers one question: is this text well-formed? It cannot tell you that `port` should be a number between 1 and 65535, or that `environment` must be one of three names. **JSON Schema** answers that second question. A schema is itself a JSON document. A validator reads the schema and a data document and reports every place where the data breaks the rules. Schemas apply to the tree from [the first lesson](/lessons/one-data-model), not to the text. That is why a JSON Schema can validate a YAML file: parse the YAML into a tree, then validate the tree. ## A first schema The course helper `schema-check` uses Ajv, which implements draft 2020-12 and asserts `format` keywords through the `ajv-formats` plugin. It prints one line per problem and exits 0 only when every file is valid. Every keyword is a small test, and a document must pass all of them. `type` checks the kind of value. `properties` attaches a sub-schema to each named key. `required` lists keys that must be present. `additionalProperties: false` rejects any key not named in `properties`. `enum` lists the allowed values. ## Reading the errors With `allErrors` turned on, the validator reports every failure rather than stopping at the first. Each line is `file`, then a JSON Pointer to the offending part of the data, then the message. `(root)` means the whole document, and `/port` means the `port` key. Four problems, four lines. The message for `additionalProperties` names the offending key, and the message for `enum` lists the allowed values. A pointer such as `/items/2/qty` means "key `items`, element 2, key `qty`", counting from zero. ## Validating YAML The tree is what gets validated, so the data file can be YAML. `schema-check` parses files ending in `.yaml` or `.yml` as YAML 1.2 first. The same schema file serves both formats. The string `"8080"` is not an integer, even though it looks like one. Quoting made it a string in the tree, and the schema checks the tree. Under YAML's own rules the unquoted `port: 8080` would have been a number. ## More constraints Strings, numbers, and arrays each have their own keywords: | Keyword | Applies to | Meaning | | --- | --- | --- | | `minLength`, `maxLength` | string | Length in characters | | `pattern` | string | A regular expression that may match anywhere in the string unless anchored with `^` and `$` | | `minimum`, `maximum` | number | Inclusive bounds. `exclusiveMinimum` and `exclusiveMaximum` are strict | | `multipleOf` | number | The value must be a whole multiple | | `items` | array | A schema every element must satisfy | | `minItems`, `maxItems`, `uniqueItems` | array | Size and uniqueness | | `const` | any | Exactly one allowed value | | `format` | string | Named shapes such as `email`, `uri`, `date`, `uuid` | Without `ajv-formats`, many validators treat `format` as a comment and accept anything. Draft 2020-12 allows that, so a schema that relies on `format` is only as strict as the validator running it. Check yours with a deliberately bad value, as above. ## What a schema cannot do A schema checks the shape of one document. It cannot check that a `port` is free on the host, that two services do not share a name unless you write `uniqueItems` for that, or that a referenced file exists. It also does not *fix* anything: validation never fills in defaults or converts types. Lesson 16 returns to that. ## Exercises

title: Composing schemas
summary: Reuse pieces with $defs and $ref, combine rules with allOf, anyOf, oneOf and not, branch with if/then/else, and learn why additionalProperties misbehaves next to allOf.
text: [Lesson 15](/lessons/json-schema-basics) wrote one flat schema. Real contracts repeat themselves: every service has a port, every environment has a name. Draft 2020-12 gives you ways to name a piece once and reuse it, and ways to combine pieces. ## $defs and $ref `$defs` is a holding area for named sub-schemas. `$ref` points at one with a JSON Pointer, so `#/$defs/port` means "the `port` entry under `$defs` in this document". The error points at `/admin`, the place in the data, not at the definition. The rule lives in one spot, so changing the maximum changes both properties. ## allOf, anyOf, oneOf, not | Keyword | Passes when | | --- | --- | | `allOf` | every sub-schema passes | | `anyOf` | at least one passes | | `oneOf` | exactly one passes | | `not` | the sub-schema fails | `oneOf` is the usual source of confusion. If two branches both match, `oneOf` fails, and the message says so. A document with only `url` matches the first branch and not the second, so it passes. With both keys it matches two branches, and the only message is `must match exactly one schema in oneOf`. With neither it matches none, and you also get one line per branch explaining why that branch failed (`url` missing, `path` missing) before the closing `oneOf` line. So the two failures look different: when you see only the `oneOf` line, too many branches matched, and when you see per-branch lines, none did. If you meant "at least one", write `anyOf`. `not` inverts a sub-schema and is mostly useful for forbidding a value, for example `{"not": {"const": "root"}}` on a `user` property. Because the error can only say that the inner schema matched, prefer a positive rule such as `enum` when you can. ## if / then / else Some rules depend on another field: a `tls` section is needed only when `scheme` is `https`. `if` is tested against the data. If it passes, `then` applies; otherwise `else` does. A failing `if` is not an error by itself. ## additionalProperties and allOf Suppose you extend a base shape with another. It looks natural to close the result with `additionalProperties: false`. Read the first block of output carefully. `additionalProperties` sees no `properties` beside it, so every key counts as additional, and the perfectly good `fine.yaml` is rejected. `unevaluatedProperties` instead asks which keys *any* keyword in the schema has already handled, so `name` and `port` are accepted and `extra.yaml` is the only file rejected. Note that its message, `must NOT have unevaluated properties`, does not name the key the way the `additionalProperties` message does, so you have to find the extra key yourself. The rule of thumb: use `additionalProperties: false` in a flat schema where `properties` is right beside it, and `unevaluatedProperties: false` at the top of a schema that uses `allOf`, `$ref`, or `if/then/else` to build the shape. Ajv's strict mode also asks for `"type": "object"` beside either keyword, which is why both schemas above declare it. ## Validation does not apply defaults A schema can say `"default": 8080`. That keyword is an annotation, a hint for tools that generate forms or documentation. It does not insert anything into the data, and it does not make a missing required key valid. If your program needs a default, apply it in code after validating. Ajv has an optional `useDefaults` setting that fills them in, but `schema-check` does not enable it, and a contract that quietly rewrites its input is harder to reason about than one that only reports. ## A habit for larger schemas Build up a schema one keyword at a time and keep a small set of files that should pass and a set that should fail. After each change, run `schema-check` against both sets. A schema you have only seen accept good data may be accepting everything, as the lesson 15 pitfall showed. Putting the failing examples in version control next to the schema is the cheapest regression test a contract can have, and [the capstone](/lessons/capstone) does exactly that. ## Pointing an edi

title: Converting between YAML and JSON
summary: JSON to YAML is easy. YAML to JSON drops comments, anchors, tags, and some keys. Capture exactly what is lost and how to compare results fairly.
text: Converting is mostly a question of which direction you go. JSON is the smaller format, so every JSON document has a YAML spelling. YAML is the larger one, so a conversion to JSON has to throw something away. This lesson captures what. ## Losses going to JSON A small YAML file with a comment, an anchor, a tag, and a second document shows most of it. `yaml2json` refuses a stream of several documents unless you pass `--all`. The tool stops and says the stream has two documents. JSON has no way to hold two documents in one file. With `--all` the result is an array of trees, which is a choice the tool made, not something YAML specifies. Both comments disappeared. `copy` became a full duplicate of `defaults` instead of a reference, and the way back does not restore the alias: the second YAML file has the same data, spelled out twice. If somebody edits `retries` under `defaults` in that file, `copy` no longer follows. The anchor was information about *how the author wrote it*, not about the data, and JSON has no place for it. ## Several documents `--all` is the way through. It prints one JSON array holding one tree per document, and `jq` can then take the array apart again, one compact line per document. The array is a convention of this helper. A tool that reads a stream may instead emit one JSON value per line, which is the [JSON Lines](/lessons/json-lines) format, so check what a converter does with a stream before you build on it. ## Tags and keys Tags are another thing a JSON tree cannot carry. Non-string keys are a third, because a JSON object key is always a string. Read the output slowly. The explicit `!!str` tag made `12` a string, which survived because JSON has strings. The `!Ref` tag, which AWS CloudFormation uses, was silently dropped and only the word `MyBucket` remains. The integer key `1` and the boolean key `true` became the strings `"1"` and `"true"`. The list key `[a, b]` was flattened into the string `[ a, b ]`, and Node printed a warning on stderr saying so. The key `null` became the empty string `""`. None of those conversions fail, and none changes the exit status. If your data has keys like these, check the output by eye. ## JSON to YAML is safe, with one catch Going the other way you start from the smaller format, so nothing can be lost. The catch is how the YAML is *written*. `json2yaml` uses the `yaml` package, which targets YAML 1.2, and only quotes a string when a 1.2 reader would otherwise read it as something else. Compare the three outputs. `json2yaml` quoted `"010"`, `"true"`, and `"3.10"`, but left `no`, `on`, and `1:30` bare. A YAML 1.2 reader gets the original strings back. A YAML 1.1 reader turns `no` into `false`, `on` into `true`, and `1:30` into the number `90`. Both readers are correct for their version. The practical rule: if you write YAML that another team's tool will load, quote any string that could be a boolean, a number, or a time, whatever your own writer does. [Lesson 11](/lessons/yaml-types) lists the cases. ## Comparing as trees When you test a conversion, compare trees, not text. Two files that differ only in key order or whitespace describe the same data. `jq -S` sorts object keys and prints in a fixed layout, so `diff` shows only real differences. Arrays are ordered, so `[1, 2]` and `[2, 1]` differ, and `diff` reports it. Objects are not, so `jq -S` is allowed to reorder keys. ## A conversion checklist Before you rely on a YAML to JSON step in a pipeline, ask five questions. Does the file contain more than one document? Does anything depend on an anchor staying a shared reference rather than a copy? Are there tags the downstream tool needs? Are all keys plain strings? And do any bare words, such as `no`, `on`, or version numbers, need quoting for the *next* reader? A "no" to all five means the round trip is lossless. ## Exercises

title: Reading a GitHub Actions workflow
summary: A workflow file is YAML with a few traps. See the tree GitHub receives, why the key on is special, and how to catch mistakes before you push.
text: GitHub Actions workflows live in `.github/workflows/*.yml`. They are the most common YAML file a developer edits, so they make a good test of everything so far. The file is parsed into a tree, and GitHub reads that tree: `on` says when to run, `jobs` is a mapping of job names, and each job has `runs-on` and a list of `steps`. ## The anatomy as a tree The easiest way to see the structure is to convert a workflow to JSON. Each step is a mapping. `uses` names a reusable action, `run` holds a shell command, `name` is a label, and `with` supplies arguments. A step needs `uses` or `run`, not both. Notice `pull_request:` with nothing after it. An empty value is `null` in YAML, and GitHub accepts that as "run on every pull request event". ## The key called on In YAML 1.1, the bare words `on`, `off`, `yes`, and `no` are booleans, so a 1.1 loader reads the key `on:` as `true`. In YAML 1.2 they are plain strings. GitHub's own parser reads `on` as the string, so the file works there, but another tool might not agree. If a script of yours loads workflows with a 1.1 library, it will look for a `"on"` key and find `"true"`. The fix is in your script, not in the workflow: either use a 1.2 parser or handle both spellings. Writing `"on":` with quotes in the workflow also works on both, but most people leave it bare. ## Expressions are strings `${{ ... }}` is GitHub's expression syntax. YAML does not know about it, so the parser sees an ordinary scalar, and the dollar sign and braces are legal inside a plain scalar when it starts with `$`. A value that *starts* with `{` would be a different story: YAML would try to read a flow mapping. A leading `*` starts an alias in YAML, so the unquoted glob is an error: the parser looks for an anchor named `.js` and finds none. Quoting `'*'` is the standard answer. The unquoted `{{ a.b }}` is worse because it is *not* an error. A value that starts with `{` is read as a flow mapping, so `x` becomes a mapping with one key, `{ a.b }`, whose value is null. The file parses and the meaning is wrong. GitHub's `${{ }}` form avoids this because the value starts with `$`, but a bare `{{ }}` copied from a templating language does not. The `:` in a plain scalar is only special when followed by a space, which is why `3:1` can be left bare, but quoting it makes the intent clear. (`yamlcheck`, the course's checker, reports `unquoted-glob.yml` as fine, because it only looks at parse errors and the alias problem appears when the data is built. `yaml2json` builds the data, so it catches it. Run the converter as well when you want to be sure.) ## Multi-line commands For anything longer than one line, use a literal block scalar (`|`). Every line is kept exactly, including newlines, and the shell receives it as one script. The first command is two lines, and the second is one line, because `>` folds line breaks into spaces. For a shell script you almost always want `|`. See [lesson 10](/lessons/yaml-scalars) for the chomping indicators that control the final newline. ## needs and if Jobs run in parallel unless one names another in `needs`. A step or job can carry an `if` condition, which is again a string that GitHub evaluates later. The `if` value is a string to the parser, as the `type_of_if` field shows. Inside it, the single quotes belong to GitHub's expression language, and YAML passes them through untouched. Because a plain scalar cannot start with certain characters, an `if` that begins with `!` or `{` must be quoted or wrapped in `${{ }}`. ## Matrices A matrix is a mapping from a name to a list of values, and GitHub runs the job once per combination. The schema above is a small hand-written one for this lesson, not GitHub's own. It checks that `on` and `jobs` exist, that every job has `runs-on`, and that every step has `uses` or `run`. It catches structural slips, but not a misspelt expression or a wrong action name. For fuller checking, use a dedicated workflow linter. ## Exercises

title: Config files in the wild
summary: package.json, tsconfig.json, Docker Compose, and Kubernetes manifests each use these formats a little differently. Read them as trees and know which parser each expects.
text: By now you can read the tree behind any one file. This lesson looks at four real file types and the small differences in how each tool reads its format. ## package.json is strict `npm` reads `package.json` with an ordinary JSON parser. There are no comments, no trailing commas, and no single quotes. People often want a comment in it, and the common workaround is a made-up key such as `"//": "note"`, which npm ignores. Node's `JSON.parse` follows RFC 8259, so it stops at the first thing the grammar does not allow, which here is the `//` comment on line 3, and the script exits with status 1. The message gives a position, which is the same information [lesson 2](/lessons/json-grammar) taught you to use. Fixing the comment would only reveal the next problem, the trailing comma after `"index.js"`. The `"//"` workaround keeps the file strict: It is an ordinary key whose value nobody reads. That is why it works in a strict parser and also why it is a convention, not a feature. ## tsconfig.json is JSONC The TypeScript compiler reads `tsconfig.json` with its own parser, which accepts comments and trailing commas. This is sometimes called JSONC, "JSON with comments". It is a dialect, not a standard: the TypeScript documentation describes what `tsconfig.json` allows, and other tools that read the same filename may be stricter. Compare what a strict parser and `jq` make of such a file. Both reject the file. If you need to process a `tsconfig.json` in a script, strip the comments first with a tool that understands JSONC, or ask the TypeScript API to parse it, instead of running `jq` on it directly. ## Docker Compose is YAML A Compose file is a YAML mapping. Its `services` key maps service names to settings, and `ports` is a list. Here the YAML types matter, because Compose reads port numbers that look like times. `"8080:80"` is quoted, and the output shows it as a string. That matters, because an unquoted `22:22` can be read as something else, as the next example shows. `DEBUG` is quoted too, so it is the string `"false"`, whereas `WORKERS` is a number. Environment variables are strings once they reach a process, so quoting a value that looks like a boolean or number states your intent. Under YAML 1.2 every entry is a string. Under 1.1 the first becomes the number 1342, because `22:22` is read as base 60 (22 × 60 + 22), while `8080:80` stays a string since `80` is not a valid base-60 digit group. The quoted entry is safe both ways. That is why the Compose documentation advises quoting port mappings. ## Kubernetes: many documents in one file A Kubernetes manifest often holds several objects separated by `---`. Each document has `apiVersion`, `kind`, and `metadata`. That is exactly what `--all` is for, and `jq` can then filter the array. Note that `RETRIES: "3"` is quoted. In a `ConfigMap`, `data` values must be strings, so an unquoted `3` would be a number and the cluster would reject it. That is a YAML typing issue the converter makes visible: convert and look for numbers where you meant strings. ## Numbers that should be strings Identifiers that happen to be digits are a steady source of bugs: zip codes, phone numbers, version strings, build numbers. The unquoted `02134` loses its leading zero and `1.10` loses its trailing one, because the parser built numbers. The quoted `"0042"` kept its zeros. If a value is an identifier rather than a quantity, quote it in YAML and use a JSON string in JSON. Nothing is wrong with the parser. It did what the grammar says, and the type is the author's decision to make explicit. ## Choosing a format When you design a config file for your own tool, the decision is usually small. - **JSON** when machines write it, when every parser must agree, or when you want no surprises. It has one dialect and no implicit types beyond the six. - **YAML** when humans edit it by hand and want comments, anchors, or less punctuation. You accept the typing rules of [lesson 11](/lessons/yaml-types) and the safety care of [les

title: Capstone, a validated config pipeline
summary: Put the course together. A YAML file with anchors, a JSON Schema, a jq summary, and a shell check that fails the build on bad input.
text: The pipeline in this lesson has four stages: **parse**, **validate**, **check relationships**, **summarise**. It uses nothing new, only the tools from the earlier lessons, and its job is to turn a hand-edited YAML file into something a script can trust. ## The data The file describes services. Two reusable resource sizes are defined once with anchors, and each service points at one. Whole-value aliases like these work under YAML 1.2, which is what `yaml2json` reads by default. Read the summary line for `prod`. It multiplies each service's replicas by its memory, which only works because the anchors were expanded: `worker.resources.memory_mb` exists even though the YAML never spelt it out. That is what [lesson 17](/lessons/converting) meant by "anchors become copies". Here the copy is exactly what you want. ## The check script A schema covers one document's shape. It cannot say that two services must not share a port. That belongs in a small script, and the script is also where you decide the order of the layers and the exit status. This one runs in CI style: it reports every problem it can, then exits 1 if there was any. Four files, four outcomes. `good.yaml` passes. `clash.yaml` is perfectly valid against the schema, and only the script's own port check catches it. `invalid.yaml` fails the schema twice, and `malformed.yaml` fails at the first stage, so no later stage runs on text that is not YAML. In CI, you would run `bash check.sh services.schema.json services.yaml` as one step, and a non-zero exit would stop the pipeline. The `&&` and `||` in the loop turn the exit status into a printed label, so the script as a whole still succeeds and the capture shows all four results. ## Why the script is shaped this way A few small decisions in `check.sh` are worth copying. **Stop early only when later stages would be meaningless.** A malformed file has no tree, so the script exits straight after the parse stage. A schema failure, by contrast, does not stop the port check, because the data is still readable and a developer fixing a file would rather see every problem in one run than fix them one at a time. **Run the converter as well as the checker.** `yamlcheck` reports parse errors, but as [lesson 18](/lessons/github-actions) showed, some mistakes, such as an alias to an undefined anchor, only appear when the data is built. Calling `yaml2json` and discarding its output is a cheap way to catch them. **Keep the exit status honest.** The script ends with `exit $status`, so a caller can tell success from failure without reading any text. The messages are for people, and the status is for the pipeline. **Tolerate missing keys in the relationship check.** The `?` in `.services[]?` stops `jq` from failing on a file with no `services` list, so that case is left for the schema to report instead of producing a confusing `jq` error. ## Running it in CI In a GitHub Actions workflow this is one step. The YAML below is only an illustration of where the command goes, and it assumes the helpers are installed on the runner: If the command exits non-zero, GitHub marks the step failed and later steps are skipped by default. Nothing in the YAML knows about your schema. The checking happens entirely in the command, which is the point of keeping the pipeline in a script you can also run on your own machine. ## Where to go from here You now have every piece: the tree model, the two syntaxes, the typing rules and their traps, the conversion losses, and a contract language. When you meet a new config format, ask the same questions in order. Which parser reads it, and for which YAML or JSON dialect? What tree does it build? What does the schema, if any, require? And what rule falls outside what a schema can say? The [playground](/playground) is a quick place to try a snippet when you are unsure how a parser will read it. ## What each layer caught | File | Parse | Schema | Own check | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | `good.yaml` | ok | ok | ok | | `clash.yaml` |
